title: Still Have Pain After Knee Replacement? What Is Normal and When to Get It Checked
metaDescription: Pain, swelling or stiffness months after knee replacement? What the evidence says is normal, how long it lasts, and which symptoms need checking.
intro: Most people are far more comfortable after a knee replacement than they were before it. But recovery is slower than many expect, and some ache and swelling at three months is common rather than a sign that something has gone wrong. This page explains what the evidence says is normal, what is not, and which symptoms need to be seen quickly.

sections.heading: Is it normal to still have pain after knee replacement?
sections.body: In the first few months, yes. A 2025 systematic review in BMJ Open found that about 22% of people still report troublesome pain three months after knee replacement, and about 12–15% have longer-term pain up to two years. So early pain is common; pain that lasts is a minority. The review is honest about its limits: the studies it pooled defined pain in different ways, and the authors rated their confidence in the figures as low. Treat these numbers as a guide to what is common, not a prediction for your knee. Most people are not in the long-term group, and pain usually eases steadily over the first year.

sections.heading: How long do pain and swelling usually last?
sections.body: Swelling is usually the slowest thing to settle. OrthoInfo (from the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons) says moderate to severe swelling is common in the first few days or weeks, and mild to moderate swelling can last about three to six months. Pain generally eases over months rather than weeks. What matters most is the direction: a knee that is slowly getting better is usually on track; one that is getting worse is not.

table.caption: What is common after knee replacement, and what needs checking
rows: Moderate to severe swelling; soreness that needs regular painkillers
Calf or leg pain and swelling, breathlessness, chest pain, fever, a red or oozing wound
Mild to moderate swelling, often worse by evening; aching after exercise; about 1 in 5 people still report troublesome pain at 3 months
Pain or swelling that is getting worse rather than better; a bend that has stopped improving
For most people pain has largely settled
Pain that has not improved, new pain in a knee that had been comfortable, or increasing stiffness

sections.heading: Why does my knee still hurt months after surgery?
sections.body: Often there is no single fault: the knee is still recovering from a major operation, and swelling and muscle weakness take time to settle. But persistent pain can also have a specific cause, which is why it should be assessed rather than simply put up with. Possible causes include:
bullets: Stiffness, or weakness of the thigh muscles that support the knee.
Infection, which OrthoInfo notes can appear months or even years after surgery, sometimes as increased pain or stiffness in a knee that had been doing well.
Loosening or wear of the implant, which is uncommon.
Irritation of the nerves around the knee.
Pain coming from somewhere else, such as the hip or the lower back, and felt in the knee.

sections.heading: Is stiffness after knee replacement a problem?
sections.body: Some stiffness is expected while the knee heals, and the NHS lists ongoing stiffness and difficulty bending among the possible longer-term problems after knee replacement. The bend usually improves with physiotherapy over the first months. If it stops improving, tell your surgeon early rather than waiting, because stiffness is easier to deal with before it sets in. OrthoInfo advises continuing your prescribed exercises for at least two months after surgery. Keep going even after the wound has healed: the bend and strength you build in these months are what the knee keeps.

sections.heading: Which symptoms mean I should be seen quickly?
sections.body: Some symptoms are not part of normal recovery. After a recent knee replacement, the NHS advises getting urgent medical advice for the following, and emergency care if leg pain or swelling comes with breathlessness or chest pain:
bullets: Throbbing or cramping pain in the leg (a possible blood clot).
A high temperature, or feeling hot, cold or shivery.
Oozing or pus from the wound.
Redness, tenderness, swelling or pain in the knee that is getting worse rather than better.
Breathlessness or chest pain: go to emergency care immediately.

Later on, even months or years after surgery: pain that does not change with activity, redness and swelling at the incision, wound drainage, or increased pain or stiffness in a knee that had been working well. OrthoInfo lists these as possible signs of infection.

sections.heading: What should I do if my pain is not settling?
sections.body: Go back to your surgeon. Persistent pain after knee replacement is worth assessing even if the operation went well, because sometimes a treatable cause is found, and if none is, the pain can still be managed. An examination and an X-ray, sometimes with blood tests, are the usual starting point. It helps to note when the pain is worst, whether it comes at rest or only with activity, and whether the knee is getting more swollen or stiff. Often the answer is targeted physiotherapy and time; a further operation is considered only when a specific, fixable cause is found.

faqs.q: How long does pain last after knee replacement?
faqs.a: It usually eases over months rather than weeks. A 2025 BMJ Open review found about 22% of people still report troublesome pain at three months, and about 12–15% have longer-term pain up to two years.

faqs.q: Is swelling normal 3 months after knee replacement?
faqs.a: Yes. OrthoInfo says mild to moderate swelling can last about three to six months. Swelling that is increasing, or comes with redness, fever or wound discharge, should be checked.

faqs.q: Why is my knee replacement still stiff?
faqs.a: Some stiffness is expected while the knee heals, and keeping up your physiotherapy exercises matters. If the bend stops improving, tell your surgeon early rather than waiting.

faqs.q: Can a knee replacement get infected months or years later?
faqs.a: Yes, though it is uncommon. OrthoInfo notes infection can appear months or even years after surgery, sometimes as increased pain or stiffness in a knee that had been doing well.

faqs.q: When should I worry about pain after knee replacement?
faqs.a: Get urgent advice for throbbing or cramping leg pain, fever or shivers, pus or oozing from the wound, or knee pain and swelling that is getting worse. Breathlessness or chest pain needs emergency care.
